cards.text: Jesus has been teaching about staying ready, like servants waiting up for their master to come home. Then He says something with some REAL heat on it. He has come to ignite a fire on the earth.

cards.question: Jesus says He came to ignite a fire on the earth. How does He feel about that fire being kindled?

answers.text: He wishes it were already kindled
He hopes it can wait a long time
He wants it put out quickly

cards.text: But Jesus says there's something He has to go through first. He calls it a baptism He has to undergo.

cards.question: Jesus says He feels calm and settled until that baptism is accomplished.

cards.text: Then Jesus asks, "Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth?" And friend, His answer is no.

cards.question: Jesus says He hasn't come to bring peace to the earth. What does He say He brings instead?

cards.text: Then Jesus gets specific. From now on, five in one household will be divided, three against two and two against three.

cards.question: The division Jesus describes reaches all the way between fathers and sons.
The list keeps going. Mother against daughter, and even the ___ against the ___.

cards.text: Then Jesus turns to the crowds and talks about the one thing EVERYBODY checks: the weather. They see a cloud rising in the west.

cards.question: When the crowds see a cloud rising in the west, what do they say is coming?

cards.text: And that is what happens. No app, no radar, they just look up and call it, while I check my weather app four times and STILL leave my umbrella at the bakery.

cards.question: When the south wind blows, the crowds say it will be ___, and it is.

cards.text: Then Jesus gets blunt and calls them hypocrites. They know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky.

cards.question: The crowds can read the earth and sky. What does Jesus ask why they don't know how to interpret?
Jesus tells the crowds to let someone else decide for them what is right.

cards.text: Then Jesus paints a picture: you and your adversary, on your way to the magistrate. You know that walk, friend. You're rehearsing your whole speech in your head, and so is the other guy.

cards.question: On the way to the magistrate, Jesus says to make every effort to ___ with your adversary.

cards.text: Otherwise, your adversary may drag you off to the judge, the judge may hand you over to the officer, and the officer may throw you into prison. One handoff after another, like the world's WORST relay race.

cards.question: Jesus says you'll get out of that prison before you've paid every last penny.

findings.problem: The opening card sums up the teaching before this passage (servants waiting up for their master, Luke 12:35-40) but cites only Luke 12:49. The outside fact has no reference.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The opening card says who is speaking and what is going on, but not to whom. The context gives a listener: Jesus is still answering Peter's question (Luke 12:41-42). Card 10's turn 'to the crowds' only makes sense if card 1 sets up who He was speaking to before.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The right answer 'He wishes it were already kindled' is the exact BSB wording and repeats 'kindled' from the question. The wrong answers are plain paraphrases, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Card 3 says the baptism is something Jesus has to go through 'first', so the baptism comes before the fire. Luke 12:49-50 only sets the two side by side with 'But'. It doesn't say how they connect or in what order.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Card 7 is a near-verbatim restatement of Luke 12:52 with no voice or framing from Papa Dorin.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The two-blank question asks the baker to fill in the next pairing in Jesus' list. That tests wording they haven't seen, not meaning they can reason out. 'brother' is just as reasonable a guess from the earlier cards.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Luke 12:53 gives the in-law pairing both ways ('mother-in-law against daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law'). A baker who puts 'daughter-in-law' in blank 1 and 'mother-in-law' in blank 2 is also right by the text, but would be marked wrong.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't hold together. Papa Dorin lives at his bakery on a planet just big enough for it, so 'leave my umbrella at the bakery' implies he goes somewhere else. The image also blends checking an app with forgetting to act, so the comparison is muddy next to the crowds reading the sky.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The question 'What does Jesus ask why they don't know how to interpret?' is ungrammatical and hard to read.
